We want the opposite sort of relationship. We think A's title should reflect a more general focus than B's.

choices.text: "Mayor McConnell Is Unfit to Serve" "Why Mayor McConnell Should be Reelected"
choices.explanation:
This doesn't scratch our itch from General vs. Specific, because these are equally specific.

And since these two titles really indicate a point / counterpoint relationship, they make it seem like Passage A and B were opposed to each other's main points, which seems far off.

Both A and B seemed to recognize past injustices in relation to property and to desire a rectification of that injustice.

choices.text: "Pruning Fruit Trees: A Guide for the Novice" "Easy Recipes for Beginning Cooks"
choices.explanation:
What is the relationship between these two titles? They both *kind of* relate to food?

How to prune a tree is gardening advice. Easy recipes is cooking advice. So these two titles seem to have very little topic overlap, whereas the passage had rectification of property injustice as a pretty specific overlap.

If A's title is "A Guide to Pruning Fruit Trees", then B's title should be something like, "How We Should Prune the Orange Tree in the Town Square".

choices.text: "Notable Failures of the STORM Weather Forecasting Model" "Meteorologists' Best Tool Yet: The STORM Forecasting Model"
choices.explanation:
This doesn't scratch our itch from General vs. Specific, because these are equally specific. They are both about the STORM model.

And since these two titles indicate a point / counterpoint relationship (notable failures vs. best tool), they make it seem like Passage A and B were opposed to each other's main points, which seems far off.

Both A and B seemed to recognize past injustices in relation to property and to desire a rectification of that injustice.

choices.text: "Fundamentals of Building Construction and Repair" "Engineering Report: The Repairs Needed by the Thales Building"
choices.explanation:
This captures the General vs. Specific relationship of A vs. B.

Both A and B dealt with rectification of past property injustice. Both of these titles deal with building repair.

Passage A laid out the general principles regarding property justice, and A's title here sounds like it lays out the general principles regarding building construction and repair.

Passage B dealt with a specific situation that invokes principles regarding property justice, and B's title here sound like it applies general principles of building repair to a specific situation/building.

questions.prompt: The author of passage A would be most likely to characterize the purpose of the Indian Nonintercourse Act as which one of the following?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Passage A, of course, does not directly discuss the Indian Nonintercourse Act, so we'd be wanting to re-read what we know about the I.N.A. and see if any of it sounds like it overlaps with what we know of Passage A.

The INA was a law that forced any Native American party that wanted to sell their land to a non-Native American party to first run the sale by the government, so that the government could approve its legitimacy.

The government was hoping to protect Native Americans against "fraudulent acquisition of their land holdings". It has also allowed some Native Americans a legal mechanism for pursuing ****recovery**** of lands taken from them in some illicit manner.

How does this overlap with anything in Passage A?

Well, it would certainly invoke properties of ownership and properties of transfer.

It also feels like it ties back to the ideas in Passage A of ...
*if the world were wholly just, this following definition would be all we need*
however
*some situations are not generated in accordance with the principles of justice in acquisition and justice in transfer. Some people* *****steal from others or defraud them******, for example.*

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for prevention of unjust transfers. In passage A, acquisition concerns something previously unowned; Native American lands already have owners, so the Acts safeguard concerns justice in transfer.

choices.text: legitimization of actual property holdings during the eighteenth century
choices.explanation:
The INA was meant to ensure there were legitimate ****transfers**** of actual property holdings, from Native Americans to non-Native Americans.

But this answer is saying something more like, "the INA was meant to say *whatever everyone currently has is legitimately theirs*". It definitely isn't described as having that sort of mandate.

choices.text: clarification of existing laws regarding transfer of property
choices.explanation: The Act requires federal approval for transfers of Native American land to protect against fraud. The passage does not describe this as clarification of earlier transfer laws. Nor does it establish that merely substituting enforcement for clarification would capture the Acts full purpose.

choices.text: assurance of conformity to the principle of justice in acquisition
choices.explanation: This answer seems like it would be correct if we just switched 'acquisition' to 'transfer'. Since the INA was meant to safeguard transfers of property against fraud / theft, we should be able to say that its goal was to "assure conformity to the principle of justice in transfer".

choices.text: prevention of violations of the principle of justice in transfer
choices.explanation:
The INA forced Native Americans who wanted to ****transfer**** ownership of their lands to non-Native Americans to run it by the government.

Why? Because, Passage A would say, "Some people steal from others or defraud them". Those would be violations of the principle of justice in transfer, and that's what the INA was hoping to prevent.

choices.text: implementation of a principle of rectification
choices.explanation:
The principle of rectification, as applied to Native Americans, would mean ****giving them back**** all the land that was illicitly taken (by force) by the Colonists.

The INA wasn't about giving land back to Native Americans. It had to do with Native Americans given their land away to non-Native Americans. The INA was just trying to make sure that Native Americans weren't suckered into any shady deals going forward, not trying to rectify past injustices.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the difference in approach taken by passage A as compared to passage B?

choices.text: Passage A espouses a general view without providing details, while passage B sketches an argument that it does not necessarily endorse.
choices.explanation: Passage A sets out a general account of property justice without detailing the principles conditions. Passage B introduces one natural way of reasoning about the land claims, then sketches its premises, conclusion and practical qualifications. Presenting that line of reasoning does not require attributing an unqualified endorsement of it to the author. Practical qualifications alone would not prove that the author rejects the moral conclusion.

choices.text: Passage A argues for the superiority of one view over competing views, while passage B considers only a single view.
choices.explanation: We can stop with the first ingredient here, since Passage A was neutral, dry, scholarly, and theoretical. It didn't argue in favor of any view.

choices.text: Passage A invokes commonly held principles to support a policy recommendation, while passage B relies on the views of established authorities to support its claims.
choices.explanation:
Passage A really isn't recommending anything. Or is it? It's really impossible to say for sure. The author poses a rhetorical question ("What, ****if anything****, ought to be done?") and then poses a hypothetical answer.

Passage B doesn't rely on the views of any authorities. The closest thing to authorities in Passage B would be the U.S. government or Native American tribes, but those are in the first paragraph, and Passage B doesn't really get into its "return the land" spiel until the second paragraph, at which point it just relies on common sense fairness about property.

choices.text: Passage A briefly states a view and then provides an argument for it, while passage B provides a detailed statement of a view but no argument.
choices.explanation: Passage A outlines a theory rather than first stating and then proving a view. Passage B does supply an argument: prior ownership, illicit taking and the resulting lack of current entitlement lead to a recommendation of restoration where feasible. This is reasoning, not merely an opinion or a description without an argument.

choices.text: Passage A provides an argument in support of a view, while passage B attempts to undermine a view.
choices.explanation:
It's very unclear that Passage A provides an argument in support of anything. The final sentence sounds like a recommendation, but it also sounds like the author is just explaining an implication of what a Principle of Rectification *would* say, were we to want to follow one.

Passage B doesn't set out to undermine a view. It sketches out some reasoning that agrees with in spirit but thinks in practice would involve a lot of necessary compromises.

But that's more like "qualified support" than "I'm here to undermine this view".

passages.title: Prions
passages.text:
An organism is considered to have an infection when a disease-causing agent, called a pathogen, establishes a viable presence in the organism. This can occur only if the pathogenic agent is able to reproduce itself in the host organism. The only agents believed until recently to be responsible for infections—viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites—reproduce and regulate their other life processes by means of genetic material, composed of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA). It was thus widely assumed that all pathogens contain such genetic material in their cellular structure.

This assumption has been challenged, however, by scientists seeking to identify the pathogen that causes Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), a degenerative form of dementia in humans. CJD causes the brain to become riddled with tiny holes, like a sponge (evidence of extensive nerve cell death). Its symptoms include impaired muscle control, loss of mental acuity, memory loss, and chronic insomnia. Extensive experiments aimed at identifying the pathogen responsible for CJD have led surprisingly to the isolation of a disease agent lacking nucleic acid and consisting mainly, if not exclusively, of protein. Researchers coined the term “prion” for this new type of protein pathogen.

Upon further study, scientists discovered that prions normally exist as harmless cellular proteins in many of the body’s tissues, including white blood cells and nerve cells in the brain; however, they possess the capability of converting their structures into a dangerous abnormal shape. Prions exhibiting this abnormal conformation were found to have infectious properties and the ability to reproduce themselves in an unexpected way, by initiating a chain reaction that induces normally shaped prions to transform themselves on contact, one after another, into the abnormal, pathogenic conformation. This cascade of transformations produces a plaque, consisting of thread-like structures, that collects in the brain and ultimately destroys nerve cells. Because prions, unlike other pathogens, occur naturally in the body as proteins, the body does not produce an immune response when they are present. And in the absence of any effective therapy for preventing the cascade process by which affected prions reproduce themselves, CJD is inevitably fatal, though there are wide variations in pre-symptomatic incubation times and in how aggressively the disease progresses.

Although the discovery of the link between prions and CJD was initially received with great skepticism in the scientific community, subsequent research has supported the conclusion that prions are an entirely new class of infectious pathogens. Furthermore, it is now believed that a similar process of protein malformation may be involved in other, more common degenerative neurological conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease. This possibility has yet to be fully explored, however, and the exact mechanisms by which prions reproduce themselves and cause cellular destruction have yet to be completely understood.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Prions — protein-based pathogens that cause CJD and force a rethink of what counts as an infectious agent.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy. The author lays out a long-standing assumption, describes a discovery that overturned it, and points to broader implications.

**Main Point**

Until recently scientists assumed all pathogens contain genetic material; the discovery of prions — protein agents that cause CJD by inducing other prions to misfold — has overturned that assumption and may help explain other neurodegenerative diseases.

**P1: The old assumption**

Pathogens were defined as agents that establish a viable presence in a host and reproduce there. The known pathogens (viruses, bacteria, fungi, parasites) all use nucleic acid (DNA/RNA) to reproduce, so it was widely assumed all pathogens contain genetic material.

**P2: The CJD discovery**

That assumption was challenged by research into Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a fatal degenerative dementia that creates a sponge-like brain. Investigators isolated a disease agent that lacks nucleic acid and is mainly protein. They named it "prion."

**P3: How prions work**

Prions normally exist as harmless proteins, but can adopt an abnormal shape that triggers a chain reaction — converting other prions on contact into the abnormal form. This produces destructive plaques in the brain. Because prions are naturally occurring proteins, the body doesn't mount an immune response, and there's no effective therapy. CJD is therefore inevitably fatal, with variation only in incubation and progression speed.

**P4: Acceptance and broader implications**

The prion-CJD link met initial skepticism but is now supported by subsequent research; prions are accepted as a new class of infectious pathogen. A similar protein-misfolding process may underlie other diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, though the mechanisms aren't yet fully understood.

summaries.anotherWay:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The author is telling the story of a discovery that broke a long-held rule about what infections look like — and explaining how it works and what it might mean.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy. The author isn't arguing against an opponent; they're showcasing a discovery and tracing its consequences.

**Main Point**

Here's the simpler version: scientists used to think every infectious agent had to carry genetic material — DNA or RNA — because that's how all the known ones reproduce. Then researchers studying CJD found something that breaks that rule: a pathogen made mainly, if not exclusively, of protein. They called it a "prion." Prions reproduce by changing the shape of other prions on contact, producing a cascade that damages nerve cells. Because prions occur naturally in the body as proteins, the body does not produce an immune response to them. The discovery opened a whole new category of pathogen and might help explain other brain diseases too.

**P1: The old rule**

To count as a pathogen, an agent has to reproduce inside the host. Every known pathogen reproduced using DNA or RNA, so people assumed all pathogens contain genetic material.

**P2: The exception**

While hunting for the cause of CJD — a degenerative brain disease — scientists isolated something with no nucleic acid, consisting mainly, if not exclusively, of protein. They called it a prion.

**P3: How prions cause harm**

Prions are normally harmless proteins. But once one folds into the bad shape, it converts the next prion it touches into the same shape, which converts the next, and so on. That chain reaction creates plaques in the brain that kill nerve cells. Two important consequences: the body doesn't see prions as foreign (they're your own protein), and there's no therapy that stops the cascade — so CJD is always fatal.

**P4: Acceptance and a wider implication**

The prion idea was treated with skepticism at first but is now widely accepted. The author closes by noting that misfolded proteins might also play a role in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's — though the details are still being worked out.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Although most organisms are known to produce several kinds of proteins, the mechanism by which isolated protein molecules such as prions reproduce themselves is not yet known in detail.
choices.explanation: The main point includes something about research into the cause of CJD.

choices.text: Research into the cause of CJD has uncovered a deadly class of protein pathogens uniquely capable of reproducing themselves without genetic material.
choices.explanation: Paragraph 1 gives the old assumption that pathogens contain genetic material. Paragraphs 2 and 3 supply the discovery: research into CJD isolated protein-based prions without nucleic acid and explained their unusual reproduction. Together these support the main point in B.

choices.text: Recent research suggests that prions may be responsible not only for CJD, but for most other degenerative neurological conditions as well.
choices.explanation: Prions may be responsible for some other neurological conditions (fourth paragraph), but to say that prions are responsible for most of them goes too far.

choices.text: The assertion that prions cause CJD has been received with great skepticism in the scientific community because it undermines a firmly entrenched view about the nature of pathogens.
choices.explanation: The assertion was met with great skepticism, but (fourth paragraph), but the passage does not indicate why. Furthermore, the way the assertion was met in the scientific community is subordinate to the discovery itself.

choices.text: Even though prions contain no genetic material, it has become clear that they are somehow capable of reproducing themselves.
choices.explanation: The main point includes something about research into the cause of CJD.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body: It's an *Undefined Target* so there's no research to do.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Find the most provable answer. Weaker claims are more provable, so use strength of language as an initial means of prioritizing which answers to research in the passage.

choices.text: Understanding the cause of CJD has required scientists to reconsider their traditional beliefs about the causes of infection.
choices.explanation:
This is charmingly related to the main point of this Old / New passage.

OLD - the only agents that can cause infections have genetic material (nucleid acid) in their cellular structure.

NEW - Oops, our bad. There's actually another infection causing agent called prions, and it doesn't have nucleid acid.

P1 says it was "widely assumed that all pathogens contain such genetic material."

P2 opens with "This assumption has been challenged" by CJD research.

P4 confirms the prion theory is now supported and represents "an entirely new class of infectious pathogens."

choices.text: CJD is contagious, though not highly so.
choices.explanation: The passage doesn't address whether or how readily CJD is transmitted between people. It describes how prions reproduce inside the body, not transmission routes between hosts.

choices.text: The prevention of CJD would be most efficiently achieved by the prevention of certain genetic abnormalities.
choices.explanation: The passage discusses prions as proteins that adopt an abnormal conformation, but it doesn't link CJD prevention to specific genetic abnormalities. P3 even notes there is no effective therapy currently. There is no claim about preventing CJD by addressing genetic abnormalities.

choices.text: Although patients with CJD exhibit different incubation times, the disease progresses at about the same rate in all patients once symptoms are manifested.
choices.explanation: P3 says explicitly that "there are wide variations in pre-symptomatic incubation times and in how aggressively the disease progresses." So the disease does not progress at the same rate in all patients once symptoms manifest.

choices.text: The prion theory of infection has weak support within the scientific community.
choices.explanation: P4 says explicitly that subsequent research "has supported the conclusion that prions are an entirely new class of infectious pathogens." Initial skepticism gave way to acceptance. So the prion theory does not have weak support; it has strong support.

choices.explanation: The passage does not discuss how a physical blow would impact the development of CJD.

choices.text: Does the patient experience occasional bouts of insomnia?
choices.explanation: Insomnia could be due to other causes.

choices.text: Has the patient been exposed to any forms of radiation that have a known tendency to cause certain kinds of genetic damage?
choices.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes the isolated CJD agent as lacking nucleic acid, and paragraph 3 describes reproduction through changes in protein shape. The passage does not connect radiation-induced genetic damage with diagnosing CJD.

choices.text: Has any member of the patient's immediate family ever had a brain disease?
choices.explanation: The passage does not suggest there are hereditary causes of CJD.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
It's a totally *Undefined Target*, so we just have to dive into the answers, looking for the most provable claim.

Weaker claims are easier to prove/support, so we'll prioritize considering/researching any answers that make weaker claims.

choices.text: The only way in which CJD can be transmitted is through the injection of abnormally shaped prions from an infected individual into an uninfected individual.
choices.tag: Too Strong (the only) / Out of Scope (modes of transmission)
choices.explanation:
The passage doesn't mention how CJD is transmitted at all.

And it's a huge turn-off to see the extreme language that "**the only** way is via injection".

We have no support for this strong claim.

choices.text: Most infectious diseases previously thought to be caused by other pathogens are now thought to be caused by prions.
choices.explanation:
We don't want to pick an answer talking about "most X's" unless the passage ever talked about "most X's".

Did the passage ever generalize about the set of infectious disease previously thought to be caused by other pathogens?

No.

The big New idea this passage is exploring is that "we didn't realize, until we discovered prions, that a pathogen could potentially not reproduce via nucleic acid / DNA."

The New idea is not, "wow, it turns out that most diseases are caused by prions."

choices.text: If they were unable to reproduce themselves, abnormally shaped prions would not cause CJD.
choices.explanation: Paragraph 1 states a necessary condition: infection can occur only if the pathogenic agent can reproduce in the host. If abnormal prions could not reproduce, they could not establish the infection causing CJD. Paragraph 3 explains their actual reproductive cascade. This conclusion relies on the stated necessary condition, not a general rule that removing any cause must remove its effect.

choices.text: Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease are caused by different conformations of the same pathogen that causes CJD.
choices.explanation:
The passage gently speculates that "a similar process of protein malformation **may** be involved" in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, but says that the mechanisms haven't been fully explored.

We don't know for sure yet they're caused by the same pathogen.

choices.text: Prion diseases generally progress more aggressively than diseases caused by other known pathogens.
choices.explanation:
The passage doesn't compare progression rates of prion diseases against other infectious diseases.

It describe wide variation in CJD progression among patients, but that's a within-disease comparison, not a cross-disease comparison.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would be *least* likely to agree with which one of the following?

choices.text: The presence of certain abnormally shaped prions in brain tissue is a sign of neurological disease.
choices.explanation: This is supported in the third paragraph.

choices.text: Some patients currently infected with CJD will recover from the disease.
choices.explanation: The passage suggests the disease is inevitably fatal (third paragraph).

choices.text: Prions do not require nucleic acid for their reproduction.
choices.explanation: This is supported in the second paragraph.

choices.text: The body has no natural defense against CJD.
choices.explanation: This is supported in the third paragraph.

choices.text: Scientists have only a partial understanding of the mechanism by which prions reproduce.
choices.explanation: This is supported in the fourth paragraph.

questions.prompt: Given the manner in which the term "pathogen" is used in the passage, and assuming that the prion theory of infection is correct, which one of the following statements must be false?

choices.text: Nothing that lacks nucleic acid is a pathogen.
choices.explanation: The passage contradicts this statement in the second paragraph

choices.text: Prions are a relatively newly discovered type of pathogen.
choices.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes the investigations that isolated the protein disease agent and coined the term prion; paragraph 4 describes its initially skeptical reception and subsequent support.

choices.text: All pathogens can cause infection.
choices.explanation: This is supported in the first paragraph.

choices.text: Pathogens contribute in some manner to the occurrence of CJD.
choices.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 identify prions as the CJD pathogen and explain how their cascade destroys nerve cells. The first paragraph only defines infection and describes the earlier general assumption.

choices.text: There are other pathogens besides viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites.
choices.explanation: This is supported in second paragraph.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the claim that prions cause CJD?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
First we would want to revisit what the support is for the hypothesis that CJD is caused by prions.

In the 2nd paragraph, we are simply told that,
*experiments aimed at identifying the pathogen responsible for CJD have led surprisingly to the isolation of a disease agent [that they eventually named 'prion'].*

Okay, so there's not really an **argument** being made, more of just a claim.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
If we're going to undermine the plausibility, we're probably looking for something like

- *Cause / No effect*
These people have abnormal prions, but not CJD

- *No Cause / Effect*
These people have CJD, but their prions are normal

- *Some other mismatch*
Take something we know about prions and something we know about CJD and make them mismatch (CJD usually starts around age 30, but prions don't take on their abnormal shape until age 50).

choices.text: Several symptoms closely resembling those of CJD have been experienced by patients known to have a specific viral infection.
choices.explanation: Having common symptoms is too weak to establish that CJD has a common cause as viral infections.

choices.text: None of the therapies currently available for treating neurological diseases is designed to block the chain reaction by which abnormal prions are believed to reproduce.
choices.explanation: A lack of available treatment does not suggest the cause of the disease. We only recently discovered prions, so it would be unsurprising if there aren't drugs or therapies developed and disseminated for it yet.

choices.text: Research undertaken subsequent to the studies on CJD has linked prions to degenerative conditions not affecting the brain or the central nervous system.
choices.explanation: A link to other degenerative conditions does not undermine the claim that prions cause CJD. The answer does not say prions affect only those other tissues. It need not independently establish or strongly strengthen the particular CJD link to be eliminated here.

choices.text: Epidemiological studies carried out on a large population have failed to show any hereditary predisposition to CJD.
choices.explanation: The absence of a hereditary predisposition does not count against the protein-pathogen hypothesis. The passage does not establish that heredity and prions would be mutually exclusive causes, so ruling out hereditary predisposition would not by itself prove or strengthen a prion explanation.

choices.text: A newly developed antibacterial drug currently undergoing clinical trials is proving to be effective in reversing the onset of CJD.
choices.explanation:
If an anti-bacterial medicine helps to reverse the onset of CJD, this would suggest that the cause of CJD was bacterial, not prions.

Prions are a 5th type of pathogen, whereas bacteria were one of the four previously known kinds.

passages.title: Katherine Dunham
passages.text:
One of the more striking developments in modern North American dance was African American choreographer Katherine Dunham’s introduction of a technique known as dance-isolation, in which one part of the body moves in one rhythm while other parts are kept stationary or are moved in different rhythms. The incorporation of this technique into North American and European choreography is relatively recent, although various forms of the technique have long been essential to traditional dances of certain African, Caribbean, and Pacific-island cultures. Dunham’s success in bringing dance-isolation and other traditional techniques from those cultures into the mainstream of modern North American dance is due in no small part to her training in both anthropological research and choreography.

As an anthropologist in the 1930s, Dunham was one of the pioneers in the field of dance ethnology. Previously, dance had been neglected as an area of social research, primarily because most social scientists gravitated toward areas likely to be recognized by their peers as befitting scientifically rigorous, and therefore legitimate, modes of inquiry. Moreover, no other social scientist at that time was sufficiently trained in dance to be able to understand dance techniques, while experts in dance were not trained in the methods of social research.

Starting in 1935, Dunham conducted a series of research projects into traditional Caribbean dance forms, with special interest in their origins in African culture. Especially critical to her success was her approach to research, which diverged radically from the methodology that prevailed at the time. Colleagues in anthropology advised her not to become too closely involved in the dances she was observing, both because of the extreme physical demands of the dances, and because they subscribed to the long-standing view, now fortunately recognized as unrealistic, that effective data gathering can and must be conducted from a position of complete detachment. But because of her interest and her skill as a performer, she generally eschewed such caution and participated in the dances herself. Through prolonged immersion of this kind, Dunham was able not only to comprehend various dances as complex cultural practices, but also to learn the techniques well enough to teach them to others and incorporate them into new forms of ballet.

Between 1937 and 1945, Dunham developed a research-to-performance method that she used to adapt Caribbean dance forms for use in theatrical performance, combining them with modern dance styles she learned in Chicago. The ballets she created in this fashion were among the first North American dances to rectify the exclusion of African American themes from the medium of modern dance. Her work was thus crucial in establishing African American dance as an art form in its own right, making possible future companies such as Arthur Mitchell’s Dance Theater of Harlem.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Katherine Dunham’s influence on modern North American dance through her introduction of dance-isolation and adaptation of Caribbean and African dance forms.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy

**Main Point**

Katherine Dunham, drawing on her dual backgrounds as an anthropologist and choreographer, revolutionized North American dance by introducing dance-isolation and incorporating traditional dance forms from African, Caribbean, and Pacific cultures, laying the groundwork for greater recognition of African American dance. **The Most Valuable Sentence appears at the end of paragraph 1:** “Dunham’s success in bringing dance-isolation and other traditional techniques from those cultures into the mainstream of modern North American dance is due in no small part to her training in both anthropological research and choreography.”

**P1: Introduction of Dance-Isolation and Dunham’s Unique Perspective**

Katherine Dunham’s key innovation, dance-isolation, brought a new movement technique from African, Caribbean, and Pacific cultures into the mainstream of North American dance. Her ability to do so is attributed to her background in both anthropology and choreography.

**P2: Status of Dance Research before Dunham / Challenges**

Before Dunham, dance was largely ignored by social researchers due to a lack of credibility in the field and a shortage of scholars trained in both dance and research. Dunham was exceptional because she understood both worlds.

**P3: Dunham’s Research Methods and Impact**

Dunham began studying traditional Caribbean dance in 1935, bucking the academic trend of detached observation by immersing herself physically in the dances. By participating directly, she both understood the cultural context and learned to teach these techniques, eventually blending them into ballet.

**P4: Dunham’s Artistic Achievements and Lasting Influence**

By adapting Caribbean dance with modern techniques, Dunham created some of the first North American ballets to feature African American themes, helping to legitimize African American dance as a respected art form and paving the way for future dance companies.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The central topic of the passage is *Katherine Dunham*.

Why was the author writing about her? What framework did we use? What would be the *one* sentence the author could say about her, if he could only communicate one thing to us?

We probably used a *Highlight Noteworthy* framework, since this is mainly a glowing, informative article about someone.

So combining *Highlight Noteworthy* + *Katherine Dunham*, our main point should sound like whatever our author was stressing was distinctive, important, or interesting about her.

The first sentence calls her introduction of "dance-isolation" *one of the more **striking** (i.e. Noteworthy) developments in modern American Dance.*

So the main point will probably center around Dunham introducing dance isolation. Why is she or it noteworthy?

The final sentence of the first paragraph sounds like it answers the former: Dunham's success was probably crucially reliant on her training in both anthropological research and choreography.

This idea gets fleshed out in the 2nd paragraph (which affirms that it's an important idea). Dunham was noteworthy for being an one of the first anthropologists to take on dance, and she was uniquely qualified to understand it because she was also trained in dance.

The 3rd paragraph mentions that Dunham was distinctive because she got immersed in the dances she was studying (rather than staying detached).

And the 4th paragraph highlights how she then taught these foreign dance styles in America, crucially establishing African American dance as an art form in its own right.

Okay ... like so many Highlight Noteworthy passages, it's hard to limit ourselves to which of these details is most "main point"-worthy.

Let's look for something praising her for introducing dance isolation, and highlighting any of her distinct or noteworthy attributes:
- studied dance when others didn't
- knew how to dance when others didn't
- got immersed in her subject, while others wouldn't
- helped establish African American dance as its own art form

choices.text: Katherine Dunham transformed the field of anthropology by developing innovative research methodologies for studying Caribbean and other traditional dance styles and connecting them with African American dance.
choices.tag: Too Strong: transformed anthropology / Out of Scope: innovative methodologies
choices.explanation:
This starts off way too strong. We never heard that she **transformed** the field of anthropology, just that she studied things others weren't and operated in ways that others didn't.

She didn't develop *multiple* innovative research methodologies for studying Caribbean / other traditional dance styles.

She studied Caribbean / other traditional dance styles, and her methodology was atypical in that she got directly involved in learning those dance styles.

choices.text: Katherine Dunham's ballets were distinct from others produced in North America in that they incorporated authentic dance techniques from traditional cultures.
choices.explanation:
Was the central topic of this passage, *Dunham's **ballets**?*

Her ballets get mentioned in the final paragraph, but the author never said they were unique because they incorporated authentic dance techniques from traditional cultures. They did do that, but the author never said that other ballets in North America *didn't* do that.

Instead, the big ideas were Dunham / dance isolation / one of the first and most qualified to study dance ethnology / got unusually involved in what she was studying / established African American dance as its own art form.

None of those central themes are captured in this answer.

choices.text: Katherine Dunham's expertise as an anthropologist allowed her to use Caribbean and African dance traditions to express the aesthetic and political concerns of African American dancers and choreographers.
choices.explanation: Nothing in the passage ever says that she used dance traditions to express the **political** concerns of African American dancers and choreographers.

choices.text: The innovative research methods of Katherine Dunham made possible her discovery that the dance traditions of the Caribbean were derived from earlier African dance traditions.
choices.explanation:
The passage never said that Dunham *discovered* that dance traditions of the Caribbean were derived from earlier African ones.

The first paragraph says, "various forms of the [dance-isolation] technique have long been essential to traditional dances of certain African, Caribbean, and Pacific-island cultures".

She was notable for being able to pull this (and other traditional techniques) into the mainstream, but the passage never gives her credit for discovering the origin story of Caribbean dance traditions.

choices.text: Katherine Dunham's anthropological and choreographic expertise enabled her to make contributions that altered the landscape of modern dance in North America.
choices.explanation:
Of the available options, this best captures why she is *Noteworthy:*

- her introduction of dance-isolation was "one of the more **striking** developments in modern North American dance"

This supports the language that she "altered the landscape of modern dance in North America". The final paragraph also gives us ammunition for that:

- the ballets she created were "among the **first** North American dances to rectify the exclusion of African American themes from the medium of modern dance".

The end of the 1st paragraph spotlights the causal difference-maker that allowed Dunham to play this pivotal role: *her training in both anthropological research and choreography*.

We learn in the 2nd paragraph that almost no one had the *dual*-expertise of knowing both anthropology and dance. We learn in the 3rd paragraph, that "because of her interest and her skill as a performer" she was able to eschew the usual detachment of anthropologists and instead get directly involved with her subject of inquiry.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, Dunham's work in anthropology differed from that of most other anthropologists in the 1930s in that Dunham

choices.text: performed fieldwork for a very extended time period
related the traditions she studied to those of her own culture
employed a participative approach in performing research
attached a high degree of political significance to her research
had prior familiarity with the cultural practices of the peoples she set out to study

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the "peers" mentioned in the second sentence of the second paragraph would have been most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the study of dance?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
We're hunting in the text for, "What would these *peers* say about the study of dance?"

We are told in the 2nd paragraph that dance had been neglected as an area of study primarily because scientists only wanted to work in an area their peers were likely to recognize as befitting scientifically rigorous, thus legitimate, modes of inquiry.

So we can infer that "avoiding the study of dance" was a causal result of believing that "my peers wouldn't be likely to recognize the study of dance as befitting scientifically rigorous modes of inquiry".

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for something like, "these peers would be likely to say about the study of dance that *it's not a good candidate for scientifically rigorous inquiry / it's not a legitimate science topic*".

choices.text: Most social scientists who have attempted to study dance as a cultural phenomenon have misinterpreted it.
choices.tag: Unrelated to Goal / Too Strong: most
choices.explanation:
The only thing we can say about the peers is that they would have been likely to reject the study of dance as a rigorous field of inquiry, as a scientifically legitimate undertaking.

We have no text to support that they think "****more than 50%**** of the attempts to study dance have misinterpreted it".

choices.text: Social scientists need not be well versed in dance traditions in order to obtain reliable data about them.
choices.tag: Unrelated to Goal / Opposite, if anything
choices.explanation:
The only thing we can say about the peers is that they would have been likely to reject the study of dance as a rigorous field of inquiry, as a scientifically legitimate undertaking.

We have no text to support that they think "you can get reliable data on dance traditions without being well versed in those traditions".

To the contrary, these peers don't seem to think you can get reliable data on the study of dance, period.

choices.text: Research into dance as a cultural form cannot be conducted with a high degree of scientific precision.
choices.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains that researchers neglected dance while choosing subjects their peers would recognize as scientifically rigorous. This supports the inference that those peers doubted that research on dance could achieve a high degree of scientific precision. The answer says cannot, not can.

choices.text: Most experts in the field of dance are too preoccupied to conduct studies in the field
choices.tag: Unrelated to Goal / Too Strong: most
choices.explanation:
The only thing we can say about the peers is that they would have been likely to reject the study of dance as a rigorous field of inquiry, as a scientifically legitimate undertaking.

We have no text to support that they think "****more than 50%**** of experts in the field of dance are too busy to conduct studies."

choices.text: Dance forms are too variable across cultures to permit rigorous means of data collection.
choices.tag: Unrelated to Goal / Word Bait: rigorous
choices.explanation: The passage supports the peers doubt about scientific rigor but does not identify cross-cultural variability as their reason. Do not supply a theory about what makes research rigorous: the question asks what these particular peers would likely believe, based on the text.

questions.prompt: In the last sentence of the second paragraph, the author mentions "experts in dance" primarily in order to

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
We know that the correct answer on Local Purpose questions tends to sound like the Framing Idea that comes right before the detail we're asked about, the Takeaway that comes right after, or the gist of that paragraph.

In the 2nd paragraph, the author is telling us how Dunham was one of the first dance ethnologists. It wasn't usually studied, in part because it didn't seem like a very serious subject and in part because no social scientist understood dance well enough to study it.

The author adds that "no dance expert knew how to do social research rigorously".

The idea is that if you want to study dance as an area of social science research, then ideally you would be both knowledgeable about dance and knowledgeable about social science research.

The final sentence of the 2nd paragraph is explaining that "the people who knew social science didn't know dance / the people who knew dance didn't know social science".

(Enter: our hero, Dunham, who knows both!)

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
So the author mentions dance experts to "complete her explanation of why **previously, dance had been neglected as an area of social research**".

This is reinforcing the framing idea that came right before the detail we're asked about.

choices.text: suggest why a group of social scientists did not embrace the study of a particular cultural form
choices.explanation:
This feels pretty close, because social scientists did not embrace the study of dance, which is a particular cultural form.

And that is the big idea we're trying to connect back to.

But the detail we're being asked about is where we were told that "dance experts weren't trained in social science".

This answer is saying, "The fact that dance experts weren't trained in social science *suggests why* scientists didn't study dance."

Huh? "The fact that dance experts weren't trained in social science" *explains* why **dancers** didn't study dance as social scientists.

It doesn't seem to have any direct causal effect on whether scientists choose to study dance. (the reason why scientists didn't study dance is because they weren't sufficiently trained in dance, not because dance experts were un-trained in social science).

choices.text: suggest that a certain group was more qualified to study a particular cultural form than was another group
choices.explanation:
The passage is saying that scientists and dance experts were **equally unqualified** to study dance.

(Technically, it's not saying "equally unqualified", but we have no basis for elevating either party over the other as more qualified).

Both scientists and dance experts had 1 of the 2 things needed to study dance.

choices.text: identify an additional factor that motivated a particular social scientist to pursue a specific new line of research
choices.tag: Out of Scope: motivating Dunham / Unsupported Causal Relationship
choices.explanation:
This answer is saying, "The fact that dance experts didn't know social science well enough to study dance is one of the things that motivated Dunham to pursue dance ethnology."

We don't have anything in the 2nd paragraph that connects "dance experts' inability to study dance as a social science" to "Dunham's motivation to study it".

The passage never says that she surveyed the social science landscape, saw there were no studies of dance (since both scientists and dance experts were both unable to properly tackle it), and became motivated to study it herself.

choices.text: contribute to an explanation of why a particular field of research was not previously pursued
choices.explanation:
We were hoping for something like "complete her explanation of why **previously dance had been neglected as an area of social research**".

That's what this is saying. The fact that "dance experts didn't know social science well enough to study dance" combines with "social scientists didn't know dance well enough to study dance" in order to explain why "Previously, dance had been neglected as an area of social research".

When we pick our correct answer on Local Purpose, we love to see language that matches up with a framing idea one or two sentences prior.

choices.text: indicate an additional possible reason for the tension between the members of two distinct fields of research
choices.explanation: This answer is suggesting that there are multiple reasons why there's tension between dance experts and social scientists, but the passage is never saying that members of each of those two fields feel tension with members of the other field.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which one of the following was true of the dance forms that Dunham began studying in 1935?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The 3rd paragraph is where we talk about 1935. We had just established at the end of the 2nd paragraph that Dunham was a rare "combo talent" in the sense that she had considerable acumen in the world of dance and social science.

The 3rd paragraph shows her using those skills. Is there something in the 3rd paragraph about "dance forms". Yes, the first sentence for sure:

*traditional Caribbean dance forms, with special interest in their origins in African culture*

Later in that paragraph we can also tell they're saying these dance forms had "extreme physical demands".

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
We don't know much about these dance forms she studied in 1935, which is nice. There isn't a lot of available support text to use, so we can expect the answer to reinforce one or more of the following:

- traditional Caribbean
- origins in African culture
- extreme physical demands
- other social scientists probably wouldn't have actually engaged in learning these dance forms

choices.text: They were more similar to dance forms used in Pacific-island cultures than to any other known dance forms.
choices.tag: Too Strong: more than any other
choices.explanation:
We have no way of supporting this extreme claim that the traditional Caribbean dance forms were more similar to Pacific-island culture dance forms than to any other known dance form.

In fact, we sort of have negative support for this, since these dance forms had "their origins in **African** culture".

Africa is a continent, not an island, and it's bordered by the Atlantic and Indian Oceans, so this answer definitely isn't using 'Pacific-island' as a proxy for Africa.

choices.text: They represented the first use of the technique of dance-isolation within a culture outside of Africa.
choices.explanation:
Nothing in our available support text gives us a way to support this extreme claim that the traditional Caribbean dance forms were **the first** to ever use dance-isolation.

- traditional Caribbean
- origins in African culture
- extreme physical demands
- other social scientists probably wouldn't have actually engaged in learning these dance forms

choices.text: They shared certain rhythmic characteristics with the dance forms employed in North American ballets.
choices.explanation:
Nothing in our available support text gives us a way to support this claim that the traditional Caribbean dance forms had any commonalities with dance forms in North American ballets.

- traditional Caribbean
- origins in African culture
- extreme physical demands
- other social scientists probably wouldn't have actually engaged in learning these dance forms

choices.text: They had already influenced certain popular dances in North America.
choices.tag: Out of Support Window: popular dances
choices.explanation:
Nothing in our available support text gives us a way to support this claim that the traditional Caribbean dance forms had already influenced popular dances in North America (the passage makes it seem like when Dunham comes back, she spreads the good word about these dances and *that's* when they start to influence North America).

- traditional Caribbean
- origins in African culture
- extreme physical demands
- other social scientists probably wouldn't have actually engaged in learning these dance forms

choices.text: They were influenced by the traditions of non-Caribbean cultures.
choices.explanation:
This is the only answer to reinforce any of our support text.

- traditional Caribbean
**- origins in African culture**
- extreme physical demands
- other social scientists probably wouldn't have actually engaged in learning these dance forms

Since these traditional Caribbean dance forms had their origins in African culture, we can definitely say the African culture influenced them.

And Africa is definitely not the Caribbean, so African culture qualifies as non-Caribbean culture.

There is only one sentence in the whole passage with the keywords of 1935 and "dance forms" (the first sentence of the 3rd paragraph), and this answer is being supported purely by that sentence. When we say "find a Support Window and then be stubborn about making the correct answer come from that Support Window", we mean questions/answers like this one.

They're testing us on the sentence they're pointing us to! They found a goofy way to restate something said within that sentence. The wrong answers just pull in verbatim words / phrases from random parts of the passage. The more we're convinced that the correct answer has to use the available support text, the more likely we are to "do the work" of thinking about how the intentionally-confusing wording of this answer choice could match up with our support text.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is most analogous to Dunham's work in anthropology and choreography as that work is described in the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
How is Dunham's work in anthropology and choreography portrayed in the passage?

Towards the end of the 1st paragraph, it's saying that her success in bringing dance-isolation into modern North American dance (as a choreographer) was due in large part to her training in anthropology.

So by analogy, we could look for someone who is trained in X and Y, to use their training in Y in order to introduce some big new change in field X.

We're told in the 2nd paragraph that there was almost no one who had sufficient training in choreography and anthropology, in order to pull off what Dunham did.

So by analogy, we could look for someone who has two specialties that you wouldn't expect to overlap (i.e. the overlap should feel kind of rare / unusual / lucky).

We're told in the 3rd paragraph that Dunham eschewed the normal detached distance that anthropologists take in relation to their subjects of inquiry, instead immersing herself in what she was studying.

So by analogy, we could look for someone who you might think would be a wallflower just observing instead being an active participant.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
It's always hard to guess which traits or relationships will get used in an Analogy answer, but we can look for something like this:

A person has an unusual dual specialty many don't have (X and Y).
Because of specialty X they get really involved in learning something, even though people with specialty Y usually don't do that.
They are then able to introduce something new and cool to the field of X.

choices.text: A French archaeologist with training in musicology researches instruments used in seventeenth century France, and her findings become the basis for a Korean engineer's designs for devices to simulate the sounds those instruments most likely made.
choices.explanation:
A training in archaeology and musicology sounds like what we want.

She researches something musical / archaeological from the past. That's a little different from studying a current living culture/tradition.

And then instead of introducing something new into the field of archaeology or musicology, someone ****else**** takes her findings and does something with them. Here's where this answer really seems to stop matching up.

choices.text: An Australian medical researcher with training in botany analyzes the chemical composition of plants that other researchers have collected in the Philippines, and then an Australian pharmaceutical company uses her findings to develop successful new medicines.
choices.explanation:
This feels just like (A).

A training in medical research and botany sounds like the unusual combo of specialties.

She researches some plants that others grabbed from the Philippines. That doesn't seem like a good match for "immersed herself in actively learning something".

And then instead of introducing something new into the field of medical research or botany, someone ****else**** takes her findings and does something with them.

choices.text: A Canadian surgeon uses her skill in drawing to collaborate with a Vietnamese surgeon to develop a manual containing detailed illustrations of the proper techniques for certain types of reconstructive surgery performed in both countries.
choices.explanation:
A training in medicine and drawing sounds like an unusual combo of specialties. That's a good match.

She collaborates with someone to develop a manual. That doesn't sound like immersing herself in some active way in someone else's tradition. Bad match there.

And again we have a collaborator, which Dunham didn't have.

choices.text: A Brazilian teacher with training in social psychology conducts a detailed study of teaching procedures while working with teachers in several Asian countries, then introduces the most effective of those procedures to teachers in his own country.
choices.explanation:
A training in teaching and social psychology is a dual specialty.

He immerses herself in a different cultures practices as an active participant (working with teachers in Asian countries to understand their teaching).

And then he introduces some innovations back into one of her fields, by bring the most effective procedures home to his country.

Dunham had a dual specialty, immersed herself as an active participant in Caribbean dance in order to learn it, and then introduced something new to her field by using that stuff she learned.

choices.text: An Italian fashion designer researches the social significance of clothing design in several cultures and then presents his research in a highly acclaimed book directed toward his colleagues in fashion design.
choices.explanation:
There's no dual specialty here. This dude is just a fashion designer.

There's no immersion in some other culture's practices. He just does research, but not in the active participant sense.

But the last ingredient is okay, as he does then use this research to present something new to his field.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the colleagues mentioned in the third sentence of the third paragraph?

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body:
What do we know about these colleagues in the middle of the third paragraph? They advised Dunham *not to become too closely involved in the dances she was observing*.

These colleagues thought
- the dances are physically exhausting
- if you're trying to gather effective data, you have to do so from a *position of complete detachment*

Does the author offer any attitudinal markers showing his voice on this matter?

Yes, the author's attitude is indicated (as it so often is) with an adverb: *fortunately*.

The author says the view that "effective data gathering requires complete detachment" is a long-standing view that now has ****fortunately**** been recognized as unrealistic.

He applauds Dunham for having gotten herself involved with the dance and thus having learned it well enough to teach it to others.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: So our author would probably sign-off on something like "these colleagues are incorrect to think you need to be detached; Dunham is an example that the long-standing view is not always true". Something like that.

choices.text: They were partly correct in recommending that Dunham change her methods of data collection, since injury sustained during fieldwork might have compromised her research.
choices.explanation:
The author never indicated he was worried about injury. The author indicates that the colleagues were worried about two things:
1. dancing is too physically demanding
2. dancing would ruin your scientific detachment

The author makes a point of saying #2 is not a great reason to refrain. But that doesn't mean that by omission our author is saying that #1 *is* a good reason to refrain.

Also "physically demanding" is just exhausting, it doesn't have to include or connote the idea of "injury".

choices.text: They were partly correct in advising Dunham to exercise initial caution in participating in the Caribbean dances, since her skill in performing them improved with experience.
choices.explanation: The author endorses Dunhams departure from complete detachment but does not say that her colleagues were right to recommend initial caution because skill improves with experience. Initial caution and later improvement are not inherently contradictory; the missing element is textual support for attributing this judgment to the author.

choices.text: They were incorrect in advising Dunham to increase the degree of her detachment, since extensive personal investment in fieldwork generally enhances scientific rigor.
choices.explanation:
The author would agree with the first half of this answer, because he thinks that "maintaining detachment" was not a compelling reason to refrain from dancing.

But ... we don't know if our author is making an exception for this type of case where the thing being studied involves physical, collective movement.

Maybe the author would still say that "*extensive* personal investment in fieldwork generally *threatens* scientific rigor, but in the case of Dunham it seemed like a worthwhile learning experience to be personally invested enough to physically learn the dance."

The "****extensive**** investment + ****generally**** enhances rigor" is what's killing this answer.

Our author would sign off on
"some investment does not necessarily diminish rigor"

choices.text: They were incorrect in assuming that researchers in the social sciences are able to gather data in an entirely objective manner.
choices.explanation:
This is pulling from the line we expected:
*****fortunately recognized as unrealistic*****

The author was referring to the long-standing view that effective data gathering can and must be conducted from a position of complete detachment.

If you say, thank goodness we've finally recognized that it's ****unrealistic**** to think that "effective data gathering *can* be conducted from a position of complete detachment", you're saying, thank goodness people finally realize you can't ever really come from a position of complete detachment.

choices.text: They were incorrect in assuming that dance could be studied with the same degree of scientific rigor possible in other areas of ethnology.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: other areas of ethnology / Out of the Support Window
choices.explanation:
These "colleagues" who appear in the middle of the third paragraph never say anything about other areas of ethnology. This answer is grabbing language from outside the Support Window.

The idea of how *rigorous* something like dance research could be is covered in the 2nd paragraph.

passages.title: Happiness and Wealth
passages.text:
**Passage A**

Research concerning happiness and wealth reveals a paradox: at any one time richer people report higher levels of happiness than poorer people in the same society report, and yet over time advanced societies have not grown happier as they have grown richer. Apparently, people are comparing their income with some norm, and that norm must be rising along with actual income. Two phenomena—habituation and rivalry—push up the norm.

When our living standards increase, we love it initially but then we adjust and it makes little difference. For example, if we ask people with different incomes what income they consider sufficient, the “required income” correlates strongly with their actual income: a rise in actual income causes a roughly equivalent rise in required income. We can also look at reported happiness over time. Job satisfaction depends little on the absolute level of wages but rises if wages rapidly increase.

We do not have the same experience with other aspects of our lives. We do not foresee how we adjust to material possessions, so we overinvest in acquiring them, at the expense of leisure.

Now consider the phenomenon of rivalry. In a study conducted by Solnick and Hemenway, people were asked to choose between two options, with all prices held constant:

A. You earn $50,000 a year while everyone else earns $25,000;

B. You earn $100,000 a year while others make $200,000.

The majority chose the first. They were happy to be poorer, provided their relative position improved.

And indeed, how people compare to their “reference group”—those most like them—is crucial for happiness. In East Germany, for example, living standards have soared since 1990, but the level of happiness has plummeted because people now compare themselves with West Germans, rather than with people in other Soviet bloc countries.

**Passage B**

Does the Solnick and Hemenway study mean that we care most about one-upmanship? Perhaps out of our primeval past comes the urge to demonstrate our superiority in order to help ensure mating prospects, keeping our genetic lines going. Still programmed like this, we get unexplainable pleasure from having a bigger house than our neighbors.

This theory may sound good and is commonly heard, but it is not the explanation best supported by the evidence. Rather, the data show that earning more makes people happier because relative prosperity makes them feel that they are successful, that they have created value.

If two people feel equally successful, they will be equally happy even if their incomes differ greatly. Of course, people who earn more generally view themselves as successful. But it is the success—not the money per se—that provides the happiness. We use material wealth to show not just that we are prosperous, but that we are prosperous because we create value.

What scholars often portray as an ignoble tendency—wanting to have more than others—is really evidence of a desire to create value. Wanting to create value benefits society. It is a bonus that it also brings happiness.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The relationship between wealth, happiness, and the importance of comparison and perceived success.

**Framework**

Answer / Explain (with a dash of Present Debate on how to interpret rivalry in happiness studies)

**Main Point**

Passage A explains the income-happiness paradox through habituation and rivalry. Passage B challenges the rivalry interpretation of relative prosperity, arguing that perceived success and value creation, rather than one-upmanship, explain its appeal. (The Most Valuable Sentence is in Passage A, P1: “Apparently, people are comparing their income with some norm, and that norm must be rising along with actual income.” and in Passage B, P2: “Rather, the data show that earning more makes people happier because relative prosperity makes them feel that they are successful, that they have created value.”)

**P1 (A): Introduction of the Wealth-Happiness Paradox**

We learn that richer people in a society tend to be happier than poorer people, but as societies get wealthier, they don't necessarily get happier overall. This is because as incomes rise, so do people’s expectations (income "norms"), due to getting used to new standards (habituation) and comparing themselves to others (rivalry).

**P2 (A): How Habituation Works**

Raising living standards feels great at first, but soon people get used to it, so it no longer makes a difference; people's definition of "enough" money moves up as their income does. Job satisfaction is more about increases in pay than about absolute pay.

**P3 (A): Overvaluing Material Goods**

People fail to realize how quickly they adjust to new material possessions, so they end up overemphasizing stuff and sacrificing leisure, thinking those material gains will make them happier than they actually will.

**P4-P7 (A): The Role of Rivalry and Relative Position**

A study (Solnick & Hemenway) shows people prefer a scenario where they earn less overall if it means being ahead of others. Happiness depends on how people stack up to their peers (reference group) rather than on absolute income; for example, East Germans became less happy when they started comparing themselves to richer West Germans.

**P1 (B): Questioning the Interpretation of Rivalry**

The author asks if the desire to be better than others is all about primal competition (one-upmanship), perhaps evolved for mating advantages— but questions whether this evolutionary argument is actually correct.

**P2 (B): Rejecting the Primal Rivalry Theory**

Although the evolutionary explanation is popular, the author points out that evidence doesn’t fully support it. Instead, data suggest people are happier when relative prosperity makes them feel successful and valuable, not just "better" than others.

**P3 (B): It’s About Success, Not Money**

Money itself isn't the source of happiness—it's the sense of being successful and having created value. Even if people have different incomes, if they both feel successful, they’ll have the same happiness.

**P4 (B): Reframing Rivalry as Positive**

The author argues that striving for more isn’t just petty competitiveness—it’s often a desire to create value, which actually benefits society and makes people happier.

questions.prompt: Both passages are primarily concerned with explaining which one of the following?

choices.text: the human desire to create value
the relationship between income and happiness
the biological basis of people's attitudes toward wealth
the human propensity to become habituated to wealth
the concept of "required income"

questions.prompt: The author of passage B would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.text: The desire to demonstrate that one is wealthier than others is a remnant of human beings' primeval past.
Very few people would be willing to accept a lower standard of living in return for greater relative wealth.
Being wealthier than other people would not make one happier if one believed that one's wealth was due merely to luck.
Gradual increases in employees' wages do not increase their job satisfaction.
The overall level of happiness in a society usually increases as the society becomes wealthier.

questions.prompt: The author of passage B would be most likely to regard the conclusion that the Solnick and Hemenway study points to the existence of a "phenomenon of rivalry" (first sentence of the fourth paragraph of passage A) as

choices.text: ungenerous in its view of human nature and mistaken in its interpretation of the evidence
choices.explanation:
The 2nd half is definitely what we wanted, but "ungenerous in its view of human nature" would give me pause.

What view of human nature does the "phenomenon of rivalry" conclusion have? The first paragraph of Passage B gives us a few pieces of support:
- we care the most about one-upmanship
- we're still "programmed" by the genetic motivations of our primeval past
- we have an urge to demonstrate our superiority
- we get unexplainable pleasure from having a bigger house than our neighbors

Those definitely aren't flattering traits. And meanwhile the author's interpretation of the S&H study is just that humans care about creating value, which sounds like a more noble aspect of human nature.

Since we can point to a clear contrast in the more negative portrayal of human motivations for "phenomenon of rivalry" than the author's interpretation, it's supportable to say the other interpretation is less generous in its view of human nature.

choices.text: flattering in its implications about human nature but only weakly supported by the available evidence
choices.explanation:
Having just researched the first paragraph of passage B for the sake of (A), there's no way I want to sign off on saying that Passage A's hypothesis is *flattering* in its implications about human nature.

- care most about one-upmanship
- take pleasure in having a bigger house than our neighbors
- need to demonstrate our superiority

That sounds insufferable, not flattering.

choices.text: plausible in its account of human nature but based largely upon ambiguous evidence
choices.explanation: Passage B does not describe the study as largely ambiguous evidence for a plausible rivalry account. It rejects that account in favor of the claim that relative prosperity makes people feel successful and productive. Evidence can sometimes be ambiguous yet favor one explanation, so the rejection should rest on this author's actual characterization, not a general rule about ambiguity.

choices.text: unflattering in its implications about human nature but more or less valid in the conclusions drawn from the evidence
choices.explanation: We can be alright with the first half, for reasons summarized in (A) and (B), but the second half of this is contradicted by the author saying that *her* explanation (not the phenomenon of rivalry) is "best supported by the evidence".

choices.text: accurate concerning human nature and strongly supported by the evidence
choices.explanation: Let's not even worry about the first half being somewhat off, because the 2nd half is dead wrong. The author says that *her* explanation, not the phenomenon of rivalry, is "the explanation best supported by the evidence".

questions.prompt: Which one of the following pairs most accurately describes why the authors of passage A and passage B, respectively, mention the study by Solnick and Hemenway?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
When we're asked about the purpose of some detail, we generally find our answer by looking at the framing idea that appears right before the example.

In psg A, right before we bring up the S&H study, the author says, "Now consider the phenomenon of rivalry". This is a callback to the final sentence of her 1st paragraph: *two phenomena - habituation and **rivalry** - push up the norm*.

She's trying to explain the paradox of how people can be getting richer but feeling less happy.

The S&H study shows that we base our happiness on a comparison to our rival. So even if we're doing better than we used to be doing, we won't feel happy if we're doing *worse* than our rivals.

In psg B, the S&H study is in the opening sentence's rhetorical question. The author is asking us what our takeaway should be from the S&H study. He lays out the sort of takeaway that is similar to what psg A was thinking. But then in his 2nd paragraph he says that another explanation is better supported by the evidence (we care about creating value, and we use our relative comparisons to others as a proxy for how much value we are or aren't creating)

choices.text: to present a view that will be argued against to present a view for which additional evidence will be provided
choices.explanation:
Passage A brings up S&H to help *support* their main point, not to argue against a view. This first description makes more sense for Passage B.

Passage B isn't providing *additional evidence* for a view related to S&H. It is countering that view by offering an alternative explanation for which there is stronger evidence.

choices.text: to present a view that will be argued against to provide evidence for one explanation of a phenomenon
choices.explanation: Same as (A), Passage A brings up S&H to help *support* their main point, not to argue against a view. This first description makes more sense for Passage B.

choices.text: to provide evidence for one explanation of a phenomenon to present a view for which additional evidence will be provided
choices.explanation: Passage B isn't providing *additional evidence* for a view related to S&H. It is countering that view by offering an alternative explanation for which there is stronger evidence.

choices.text: to provide evidence for one explanation of a phenomenon to introduce the main topic to be discussed
choices.explanation:
Passage A brings up S&H to help *support* one half of the main point. The main point is that people can be richer but feel less happy because of habituation and rivalry. The discussion of the S&H study is there to explain to us how rivalry can impact our perceived happiness.

Passage B opens the passage with S&H, so it makes sense to say that it's there to introduce the main topic. The common interpretation of the S&H study is the main topic. The 2nd paragraph shows that our author's purpose in writing about this common interpretation is to challenge it and suggest that an alternate interpretation is better supported.

choices.text: to introduce the main topic to be discussed to present a view that will be argued against
choices.explanation:
The main topic of passage A is not the S&H study. The S&H study is there to flesh out the idea of how *rivalry* can impact our perception of happiness.

But the main topic is that people are comparing their income to some rising norm (via habituation and rivalry), and that's why over time advanced societies haven't grown happier as they've grown richer.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following pairs of terms would most likely be used by the authors of passage A and passage B, respectively, to describe a person who wants to make more money than his or her neighbors?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Passage B discusses this issue outright. He rejects the idea that wanting to make more than your neighbor is "an ignoble tendency, a primeval urge to demonstrate superiority in order to ensure mating prospects".

He says instead that this desire is a healthy outgrowth of our desire to create value and be a success, which are positive things.

Passage A, meanwhile, doesn't really say anything to characterize whether this propensity of ours to want more than our neighbors is good or bad. She just makes it seem like it is the norm for human psychology.
